title: Why Kubernetes, and how a cluster works
goal: By the end you can explain what each part of a Kubernetes cluster does, follow one `kubectl apply` from your terminal to a running container, and run the course's three-node cluster on your Mac with kind.

guess.q: You run `kubectl apply -f app.yaml` and it prints `deployment.apps/web created` in under a second. What has happened at that moment?
options: The containers are already running on a node
The request is stored, and other parts start the containers soon after
kubectl has copied the image to every node in the cluster
The scheduler has picked a node and waits for your approval

sections.h: The problem Kubernetes solves
sections.body:
On Day 15 you ran hello-devops and Redis with Docker Compose. One `docker compose up` on one laptop, and it worked. Now picture a real product: 40 services, several copies of each, spread over 20 servers.

Someone has to answer these questions all day:
- Which server has room for this container?
- A container crashed at 3 in the morning. Who starts it again?
- A server died. Who moves its containers somewhere else?
- Traffic doubled. Who adds copies, and who removes them later?
- How do you replace version 1 with version 2 without downtime?
- Copies come and go. How does one service find another?

Compose cannot answer them. It knows one machine, and it only acts when you run it. **Kubernetes** answers all of them. It is an open-source system that runs containers across a group of machines called a cluster. People often write it K8s: a K, eight letters, then an s.

Google built Kubernetes from what it learned running its internal system, Borg, and released it as open source in 2014. Today the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) looks after it, and every big cloud sells it.

The real change is in how you work. You stop logging in to servers and starting things. You write down the result you want, and Kubernetes keeps making it true.

sections.h: Desired state and control loops
sections.body:
With `docker run` you give an order, and Docker carries it out once. Kubernetes works the other way round. You describe the end state, and Kubernetes stores that description as your **desired state**.

Small programs called controllers then run the same loop forever:
1. Read the desired state: what you asked for.
2. Observe the actual state: what is really running.
3. If the two differ, act to make them match.
4. Repeat.

This loop is called reconciliation. The [Kubernetes docs](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/architecture/controller/) compare it to a thermostat. You set 21 degrees, and the thermostat keeps reading the room and switches the heating on or off. You never tell it to heat for ten minutes.

You can see the loop in every object. Each object you write has a `spec` field: your wish. Kubernetes fills in a `status` field: its report on what is real. Controllers work to make status match spec.

Two things follow from this, and both surprise people at first:
- Kubernetes fixes problems you never told it about. A crashed container or a dead node is just one more gap to close.
- A change made behind Kubernetes' back does not stick. Stop a container directly on a node, and Kubernetes sees the gap and starts it again.

Terraform (Part 6) also compares code with reality, but only when you run `terraform apply`. Kubernetes checks all the time, with nobody at the keyboard.

sections.h: The control plane decides
sections.body:
A cluster has two kinds of parts. The control plane stores your desired state and makes decisions. The nodes run your containers.

One word before we go on. Kubernetes never runs a bare container. It runs Pods. A Pod wraps one container, sometimes a few, and gives it an IP address. Tomorrow is all about Pods.

The control plane has four main components. For each one, it helps to ask what breaks if it stops:
- API server (`kube-apiserver`): the front door. Every request goes through it, from `kubectl` and from the other components. If it stops, `kubectl` fails, but containers that already run keep running.
- etcd: a key-value database that holds the whole cluster state. Only the API server talks to it. Lose etcd without a backup, and the cluster forgets every object.
- Scheduler (`kube-scheduler`): picks a node for each new Pod. If it stops, new Pods wait in `Pending` forever.
- Controller manager (`kube-controller-manager`): runs the built-in control loops, such as the one that keeps three copies running. If it stops, nothing heals itself any more.

Clusters in a cloud add a fifth part, the cloud controller manager. It talks to the cloud provider, for example to create a load balancer.

These components never call each other. They all read and write objects through the API server, and they watch it for changes. This design is why a component can crash, restart, read the current state again and carry on as if nothing happened.

sections.h: The nodes do the work
sections.body:
Every node runs a few programs:
- kubelet: an agent that watches the API server for Pods assigned to its node. It starts their containers, checks on them and reports their status.
- A container runtime, usually containerd: it pulls images and starts containers. The kubelet talks to it through a standard called the CRI (Container Runtime Interface).
- kube-proxy: sets up network rules so traffic sent to a Service reaches the right Pods. Day 33 explains Services.

Your Docker images run here even though the node has no Docker. A Docker image follows the OCI image standard, and containerd runs any OCI image. Kubernetes removed its built-in Docker support (called dockershim) in version 1.24, and image builds did not change at all.

A cluster also runs a few add-ons as ordinary Pods:
- CoreDNS: the cluster's DNS server, so Pods can find Services by name.
- A network plugin (CNI, Container Network Interface): it gives every Pod an IP address and connects Pods across nodes. kind uses a small one called kindnet.

One current detail matters if a cluster ever refuses to start. Linux limits the CPU and memory of containers with a feature called cgroups, which comes in two versions. Since Kubernetes 1.35, the kubelet refuses by default to start on hosts that still use the old cgroup v1. Docker Desktop on a Mac uses cgroup v2, so you are fine, and `docker info | grep -i cgroup` confirms it in seconds.

sections.h: What happens when you run kubectl apply
sections.body:
This is the most useful picture to carry around, and a classic interview question. Say you apply a Deployment that asks for two copies of nginx. A Deployment is an object that keeps a set number of Pods running (Day 32 covers it). Here is the chain:

1. kubectl reads `~/.kube/config` to find the cluster and your credentials. It sends the YAML to the API server over HTTPS.
2. The API server checks who you are and whether you may do this. It validates the object and stores it in etcd. Then it answers `created`, and kubectl exits.
3. The Deployment controller sees the new Deployment through its watch. It creates a ReplicaSet, a helper object that keeps a set number of identical Pods.
4. The ReplicaSet controller sees the ReplicaSet and creates two Pod objects. They have no node yet.
5. The scheduler sees two Pods without a node. It filters out nodes that cannot take them, scores the rest, and writes a node name into each Pod.
6. The kubelet on each chosen node sees a Pod assigned to it. It asks containerd to pull the image and start the container.
7. The kubelet reports back: the Pod is running, and here is its IP address. The API server stores that in the Pod's status.

Notice who talks to whom. Every arrow goes through the API server, and each component acts on what it sees there. Nobody sends orders to anybody. Each step also leaves a short record called an event, so you can watch the whole chain with `kubectl get events`. The worked example below does exactly that.

sections.h: Managed Kubernetes, and when to skip Kubernetes
sections.body:
In production, few teams run the control plane themselves. Keeping etcd safe, upgrading the cluster a few times a year and patching security holes is real work. Cloud providers sell managed Kubernetes instead. They run and upgrade the control plane, and you run your apps on the nodes:
- Amazon EKS (Elastic Kubernetes Service) on AWS.
- AKS (Azure Kubernetes Service) on Microsoft Azure.
- GKE (Google Kubernetes Engine) on Google Cloud.

Each one also has a mode where the provider runs the nodes too: EKS Auto Mode, AKS Automatic and GKE Autopilot.

Kubernetes still costs people time. Someone must learn it, keep it upgraded and keep it secure. Skip it when:
- You run one or a few services with steady traffic.
- Your small team has nobody to own the platform.
- A simpler service fits, such as a PaaS or serverless containers (Day 10).

A useful test: can you name the person who will upgrade the cluster next spring? If not, start with something simpler.

Your manifests work the same on kind, EKS, AKS and GKE, so practice on a laptop is real practice. The differences sit at the edges: load balancers, disks and identity.

sections.h: A real cluster on your laptop with kind
sections.body:
kind stands for Kubernetes in Docker. Each node is a Docker container that runs its own containerd and kubelet inside. The kind tool uses kubeadm, the official setup tool, to start a real control plane in the first node. So you get the same Kubernetes as a cloud cluster, minus the cloud parts.

The course uses one config file, `kind-config.yaml`, in the root of your repo. It asks for:
- One control-plane node and two workers, so you can watch Pods spread over machines.
- A port mapping from port 30080 on the control-plane node to port 8081 on your Mac. On Day 33 a Service listens on node port 30080, and `curl localhost:8081` reaches it.

When kind creates a cluster called `devops`, it writes a context called `kind-devops` into `~/.kube/config` and switches kubectl to it. A context is a saved pair of cluster and user (Day 31 shows how to list and switch them).

kind has a few limits worth knowing now:
- No cloud load balancers. A Service of type LoadBalancer waits forever unless you add a helper (Day 33).
- The nodes live inside Docker Desktop's Linux VM. Their 172.18.x.x addresses are not reachable from your Mac, so you use port mappings and `kubectl port-forward`.
- It shares your laptop's memory. If nodes turn `NotReady` or Pods get evicted, give Docker Desktop more memory in its settings.

Creating the cluster takes a minute or two, and deleting it takes seconds. You can always start fresh.

analogy: Think of a busy restaurant kitchen. Waiters never talk to cooks: they pin order tickets on a rail (the API server, with etcd as the rail's memory). The head chef reads new tickets and assigns each dish to a station (the scheduler). Each station cook makes only the dishes assigned to them (the kubelet). A manager keeps checking that every table got what it ordered, and has dropped plates remade (the controllers). The picture breaks on judgment: a real kitchen improvises when it runs out of something, while Kubernetes only ever works toward exactly what the ticket says.

code.title: kind-config.yaml
code.src:
# The course cluster: 1 control-plane node and 2 worker nodes. Each node is a Docker container.
# Create it with: kind create cluster --name devops --config kind-config.yaml
# kind then adds the kubectl context "kind-devops" and switches to it (Day 30).
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
nodes:
  - role: control-plane
    extraPortMappings:
      - containerPort: 30080 # the NodePort of the hello-devops Service (k8s/service.yaml, Day 33)
        hostPort: 8081 # so http://localhost:8081 on your Mac reaches that Service
  - role: worker
  - role: worker

mistake: Reaching past Kubernetes to fix things: `docker exec` into a kind node and stopping a container with `crictl`, or restarting a process by hand on a server. The kubelet sees the gap between desired and actual state and undoes your change, or your fix quietly disappears with the next Pod. check.q: The API server of a test cluster crashes for ten minutes. What happens to the web app that was already running there?
options: It stops at once, because Pods need the API server
It keeps serving, but nothing new can be scheduled or changed
It moves to another cluster until the API server is back
It restarts every Pod as soon as the API server returns
check.why: Kubelets keep running the containers they already have; only changes, scheduling and kubectl need the API server.

check.q: A container inside a Pod crashes. Which component notices and starts it again on the same node?
options: The scheduler
The controller manager
kube-proxy
The kubelet
check.why: The kubelet runs and watches the containers on its own node, so it restarts a crashed container in place.

check.q: A worker node loses power. Which chain of components gets its Pods running again somewhere else?
options: Controllers create new Pods, then the scheduler places them on healthy nodes
The kubelet on the dead node moves its Pods before it shuts down
etcd copies the Pods to the node with the most free memory
kube-proxy sends the Pods' traffic to another node, so no new Pods are needed
check.why: Controllers notice that Pods are lost and create replacements, and the scheduler assigns those new Pods to nodes that are still up.

interview.q: Walk me through what happens when you run kubectl apply for a Deployment.
interview.a: kubectl sends the object to the API server, which authenticates and authorizes the request, validates the object and stores it in etcd. The Deployment controller sees it through a watch and creates a ReplicaSet, and the ReplicaSet controller creates the Pod objects. The scheduler assigns each unscheduled Pod to a node, and the kubelet on that node tells the container runtime to pull the image and start the containers. Every step goes through the API server; no component calls another directly.

interview.q: What is the difference between the control plane and the worker nodes?
interview.a: The control plane makes decisions and stores state. The API server is its front door, etcd holds the data, the scheduler places Pods and the controller manager runs the control loops. Worker nodes run the workloads: the kubelet starts and watches Pods, a runtime such as containerd runs containers, and kube-proxy programs Service routing. In EKS, AKS or GKE the provider runs the control plane for you.

interview.q: What does declarative mean in Kubernetes, and why does it matter?
interview.a: You describe the end state you want, not the steps to get there. Controllers compare that desired state with what is running and keep closing the gap, so the cluster heals itself after crashes. Applying the same file twice gives the same result, which makes changes repeatable and reviewable in git. GitOps tools such as Argo CD build on exactly this idea.

deeper.body:
Every component you met today talks only to the API server. So how does the scheduler learn about a new Pod when nobody calls it?

It uses a watch. A component asks the API server for a list of objects and keeps the connection open. The API server then streams every change (added, modified, deleted) as it happens:
- The scheduler watches Pods that have no node yet.
- Each kubelet watches Pods assigned to its own node.
- Each controller watches the kinds of objects it cares about.

Controllers are also level-triggered. They act on the current state, not on a list of past events. If a controller crashes and restarts, it lists everything again and carries on. Nothing is lost, because the state lives in etcd, not in the controller's memory. This is why Kubernetes copes so well with its own parts failing.

Two fields in `metadata` will come up again:
- Every object has a `resourceVersion`. If two clients update the same object at once, the second one gets a conflict error and must read the object again. This is called optimistic concurrency.
- Objects can have owners. A Pod made by a ReplicaSet points to it in `metadata.ownerReferences`. Delete the owner, and the garbage collector deletes what it owns.

In production the control plane itself is made highly available. Teams run three (or five) control-plane nodes. The API servers are all active behind a load balancer. etcd keeps working while a majority of its members agree, so three members survive the loss of one. The scheduler and controller manager run on every control-plane node, but only one copy of each is active at a time. They pick the leader with a lock stored in the API server.

kind builds a cluster like this:
1. It starts one Docker container per node from the `kindest/node` image.
2. Inside each container, systemd starts containerd and the kubelet.
3. kind runs kubeadm, which starts the control plane parts as static Pods: Pods the kubelet runs straight from files on disk.
4. It installs kindnet and a small storage provisioner.
5. It writes a context into `~/.kube/config` so kubectl can connect.

You can watch the stream yourself. Run `kubectl get pods -w` in one terminal, then create and delete a Pod in another. Each new line is an event the API server pushed to kubectl, the same way it pushes events to controllers.

If you want to see every moving part, [Kubernetes The Hard Way](https://github.com/kelseyhightower/kubernetes-the-hard-way) by Kelsey Hightower builds a cluster by hand. It needs four machines and an afternoon, so treat it as optional reading.

title: Pods, kubectl and YAML
goal: By the end you can read and generate a Pod manifest, run your own image in a Pod on kind, explain its phase and restarts, and use the everyday kubectl commands to inspect, reach and remove it.

guess.q: A Pod's STATUS column shows `CrashLoopBackOff`. What is the Pod's phase, the value Kubernetes stores in `status.phase`?
options: CrashLoopBackOff
Failed
Running
Unknown
guess.why: `CrashLoopBackOff` is a word kubectl shows for a container that keeps crashing and waits longer between restarts. The phase stays `Running`, because the Pod is on a node and the kubelet keeps restarting its container.

sections.h: A manifest, and how to get one without typing it
sections.body:
Everything in Kubernetes is an object: a Pod, a Service, a Namespace. You describe objects in a manifest, a YAML file with four top-level fields:
- `apiVersion`: which version of the API defines this kind. A Pod is `v1`, a Deployment is `apps/v1`.
- `kind`: the type of object, such as `Pod` or `Service`.
- `metadata`: identity. The `name` and `namespace`, plus `labels` and `annotations`.
- `spec`: your desired state. Its shape depends on the kind.

You never write the fifth field, `status`. Kubernetes fills it in. A typo in a field name does not slip through, either. kubectl validates strictly by default, so `imagePullPolicyy` fails with an error that names the unknown field.

Nobody types manifests from memory. Three tricks do most of the work:
1. `--dry-run=client -o yaml` prints the object kubectl would create, without creating it. Redirect it to a file and edit from there.
2. `kubectl explain pod.spec.restartPolicy` prints the docs for one field, straight from your cluster's API, so it always matches your version. For this field it shows the type (`<string>`), the allowed values `Always`, `Never` and `OnFailure`, and a description. Add `--recursive` to see a whole tree.
3. `kubectl get pod hello -o yaml` shows a live object in full. It is longer than what you wrote, because the API server fills in defaults and `status`.

YAML has a few traps. Indent with spaces, never tabs. A `- ` starts a list item, and `containers:` is a list even with one container. Some bare words change type: `yes` and `on` can become true, and `8000` is a number. An environment variable value must be a string, so write `"8000"` in quotes.

Kubernetes 1.37 made KYAML stable for exactly this reason. It is a stricter style of YAML that quotes every string and uses brackets, so indentation cannot break it, and it is still valid YAML. Try `kubectl get pod hello -o kyaml`.

sections.h: Pods: the smallest thing Kubernetes runs
sections.body:
Kubernetes never runs a bare container. It runs Pods. A **Pod** is one or more containers that are placed on one node together and share a few things:
- One IP address and one set of ports. Containers in a Pod reach each other on `localhost`.
- Volumes, if the Pod defines them. Two containers can read and write the same folder.
- One life. They start on the same node and are removed together.

Most Pods hold exactly one container. Think of the Pod as a thin wrapper that gives your container an address and a place in the cluster. Inside the Pod, the host name is the Pod's name. That is why the `host` field in hello-devops' JSON will show the Pod name.

Pods are disposable. If a node dies, its Pods die with it, and nothing brings a bare Pod back. Delete a Pod and it is gone. A new Pod made from the same YAML is a different Pod, with a new IP address.

So you rarely create Pods yourself. You create a controller, usually a Deployment (Day 32), and it creates and replaces Pods for you. Today you make bare Pods anyway, because that is the clearest way to see what a Pod is.

sections.h: Phases, container states and restarts
sections.body:
A Pod's life is summed up in `status.phase`. There are only five phases:
- `Pending`: accepted, but not running yet. It may be waiting for a node or pulling an image.
- `Running`: on a node, containers created, at least one running or restarting.
- `Succeeded`: all containers exited with code 0 and will not restart.
- `Failed`: all containers have stopped, and at least one failed.
- `Unknown`: the node stopped reporting, so nobody knows.

A normal start shows up in STATUS as `Pending` (no node yet), then `ContainerCreating` (node chosen, image being pulled, phase still `Pending`), then `Running`.

Each container also has a state of its own: `Waiting`, `Running` or `Terminated`, with a reason such as `ImagePullBackOff` or `Completed`. The STATUS column of `kubectl get pods` squeezes all this into one word. `CrashLoopBackOff` and `Terminating` show up there, but they are not phases. Most people mix these up at first, so when STATUS looks odd, read `kubectl describe pod`.

What happens when a container exits depends on the Pod's `restartPolicy`:
- `Always` (the default): restart it, whatever the exit code. Right for servers.
- `OnFailure`: restart it only after a non-zero exit code. Right for batch work.
- `Never`: leave it stopped.

The kubelet restarts the container inside the same Pod, on the same node. It waits longer each time: 10 seconds, then 20, then 40, up to five minutes. That growing wait is the back-off in `CrashLoopBackOff`. If the container then runs for ten minutes without trouble, the wait resets.

sections.h: Init containers and sidecars
sections.body:
Sometimes your container needs a helper. Kubernetes has two kinds of extra containers for that.

Init containers run first, one at a time, in order. Each must exit with code 0 before the next one starts. Only when all of them have finished do the app containers start. Use them for setup:
- Wait until a database answers.
- Download or render a config file into a shared volume.
- Fix file permissions on a volume.

A sidecar is a helper that runs beside your app for the Pod's whole life. Typical sidecars ship logs, add TLS in front of the app, or refresh certificates. Native sidecars have been stable since Kubernetes 1.33. You declare one as an init container with `restartPolicy: Always`, and Kubernetes then:
1. Starts it in init order, before the app containers.
2. Moves on as soon as it is running, without waiting for it to exit.
3. Restarts it if it crashes.
4. Stops it only after the app containers have stopped.

That order fixes two old problems. A log shipper that started late missed the first lines, and one that stopped early lost the last ones. The READY column of kubectl counts sidecars too, so a Pod with one sidecar and one app shows `2/2`.

Put containers in one Pod only when they must share a node, an IP address or files. An app and its database belong in separate Pods, so you can scale and replace each one on its own.

sections.h: Labels, annotations and selectors
sections.body:
Labels are how Kubernetes objects find each other. A label is a key=value pair in `metadata.labels`, such as `app: hello-devops` or `tier: frontend`. A selector is a query over labels. Deployments find their Pods with selectors, and so do Services and NetworkPolicies (Day 33).

You use selectors with kubectl too:
- `kubectl get pods -l app=web` matches one label exactly.
- `kubectl get pods -l 'app=web,tier!=db'` combines rules, and all must hold.
- `kubectl get pods -l 'env in (dev,test)'` matches a set of values.
- `kubectl get pods --show-labels` prints every label, and `-L app` adds one label as a column.

Annotations look the same but have a different job. They hold notes for people and tools, and selectors ignore them. You will meet these soon:
- `kubernetes.io/change-cause`, the reason shown in a Deployment's rollout history (Day 32).
- `kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration`, which `kubectl apply` writes to remember what you applied.
- Argo CD's tracking annotation, which marks the objects it manages (Day 39).

A simple rule: if you will ever select by it, make it a label. If it is long, or only a tool reads it, make it an annotation. Kubernetes also recommends a shared set of labels, such as `app.kubernetes.io/name`, that many tools understand.

sections.h: Namespaces, kubeconfig and contexts
sections.body:
A namespace is a named group of objects inside one cluster. Names must be unique inside a namespace, not across the cluster. A new cluster starts with four:
- `default`: where objects go when you name no namespace.
- `kube-system`: the cluster's own parts, such as CoreDNS.
- `kube-public` and `kube-node-lease`: used by the system. Leave them alone.

Think of namespaces as folders, not walls. A Pod in one namespace can still reach a Pod in another over the network, and blocking that takes a NetworkPolicy (Day 33). Teams attach access rules and quotas to namespaces. Deleting a namespace deletes everything in it, which makes cleanup easy and mistakes expensive.

Which cluster does kubectl talk to? It reads a kubeconfig file: `~/.kube/config` by default, or the files listed in the `KUBECONFIG` variable. The file has three lists:
- clusters: each API server's address and certificate.
- users: your credentials.
- contexts: a cluster plus a user plus a default namespace, under one name.

One context is current, and every kubectl command goes there. `kubectl config get-contexts` lists them all and marks the current one with a star. Check it before anything risky with `kubectl config current-context`. This matters more than it sounds. Docker Desktop can run its own Kubernetes with a context called `docker-desktop`, and at work you will have contexts for real clusters. To stop typing `-n hello` on every command, set a default namespace with `kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=hello`.

sections.h: Everyday kubectl, and getting your image into kind
sections.body:
Most days you need about a dozen kubectl commands. Here they are, grouped by the question they answer:
- What is there? `kubectl get pods`. Add `-o wide` for IPs and nodes, `-w` to keep watching, `-l` to filter by label, `-A` for all namespaces.
- What happened? `kubectl describe pod hello` shows details, with recent Events at the bottom. Read the Events first.
- What did it print? `kubectl logs hello`. Add `-f` to follow, `-c` to pick a container, and `--previous` for the last crashed run.
- Let me in: `kubectl exec -it hello -- sh` opens a shell inside the container, if the image has one.
- Let me reach it: `kubectl port-forward pod/hello 8000:8000` tunnels a port on your Mac to the Pod until you press Ctrl+C.
- Remove it: `kubectl delete pod hello`, or `kubectl delete -f pod.yaml`.
- Just one field, please: `-o jsonpath='{.status.phase}'` prints a single value, which is handy in scripts.

`kubectl create -f` and `kubectl apply -f` both make objects from a file, but they think differently. The `create` command is a one-time order, and it fails if the object already exists. The `apply` command is declarative: it creates the object or updates it to match the file, so you can run it again and again. Use `apply` for anything you keep in git.

Your own image needs one more step. Each kind node runs its own containerd with its own image store, separate from Docker on your Mac. So `docker build` alone is not enough. Copy the image in with `kind load docker-image hello-devops:1.0.0 --name devops`.

Give it a real tag. With `:latest` or no tag, Kubernetes sets `imagePullPolicy: Always`, tries Docker Hub, and the Pod ends in `ImagePullBackOff`.

analogy: A Pod is like a shared hotel room. Everyone in it has the same room number (one IP address), can use the same desk (shared volumes) and checks in and out together. The init container is the cleaner who must finish before guests enter, and the sidecar is the assistant who arrives first and leaves last. The picture breaks on moving: a hotel guest can change rooms, but a Pod never moves. Kubernetes throws it away and builds a new one with a new number.

steps.say: Make a scratch namespace for experiments, so cleanup is one command later. Apply the example Pod from the lab repo. It has an init container that writes a web page, a sidecar that tails the access log, and nginx.
steps.code:
$ kubectl create namespace scratch
namespace/scratch created
$ kubectl apply -n scratch -f k8s/examples/pod-sidecar.yaml
pod/web created

steps.say: Watch the Pod start. `Init:0/2` means the first of two init containers is running. When it finishes, the sidecar starts and counts as ready (`1/2`) while nginx is still being created. Then nginx starts and READY becomes `2/2`, because READY counts the sidecar.
steps.code:
$ kubectl get pod web -n scratch -w
NAME   READY   STATUS            RESTARTS   AGE
web    0/2     Init:0/2          0          1s
web    0/2     Init:1/2          0          4s
web    1/2     PodInitializing   0          5s
web    2/2     Running           0          11s

code.title: k8s/examples/pod-sidecar.yaml
code.src:
# Day 31: one Pod with an init container, a sidecar and the main container.
# Try it in a scratch namespace:
#   kubectl create namespace scratch
#   kubectl apply -n scratch -f k8s/examples/pod-sidecar.yaml
#   kubectl get pod web -n scratch -w
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: web
  labels:
    app: web # identifying: selectors find the Pod by this
  annotations:
    example.com/owner: "team-a" # a note for people and tools; selectors ignore it
spec:
  initContainers:
    # 1. A normal init container: runs once and must exit 0 before the next one starts.
    - name: write-page
      image: busybox:1.37
      command: ["sh", "-c", "echo 'hello from the init container' > /work/index.html"]
      volumeMounts:
        - name: work
          mountPath: /work
    # 2. A sidecar: an init container with restartPolicy Always.
    #    It starts before nginx, keeps running, and stops after nginx stops.
    - name: log-tailer
      image: busybox:1.37
      restartPolicy: Always
      command: ["sh", "-c", "touch /logs/access.log && tail -F /logs/access.log"]
      volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
  containers:
    # 3. The main container: serves the page that the init container wrote.
    - name: nginx
      image: nginx:1.28
      ports:
        - containerPort: 80
      volumeMounts:
        - name: work
          mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /var/log/nginx # nginx writes access.log here, and the sidecar reads it
  volumes:
    - name: work
      emptyDir: {} # an empty folder that lives as long as the Pod
    - name: logs
      emptyDir: {}

task.title: Run hello-devops in a Pod, then break one on purpose
steps: In `~/code/hello-devops`, build the image with its version baked in: `docker build --build-arg APP_VERSION=1.0.0 -t hello-devops:1.0.0 .` Then load it into the `devops` cluster.

Generate `pod.yaml` for a Pod named `hello` with `--dry-run=client -o yaml`. Change its label to `app: hello`, add `imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent`, delete `resources: {}` and `status: {}`, and apply it.
Check the Pod with `-o wide`. Which worker did the scheduler pick, and what IP did the Pod get?
Port-forward port 8000 to the Pod and `curl localhost:8000` from a second terminal. Follow the logs in a third terminal and watch each request appear.
Open a shell in the Pod and run `hostname` and `printenv APP_VERSION`. Why does the `host` field in the JSON show `hello`?
Start a Pod that crashes: `kubectl run crashy --image=busybox:1.37 -- sh -c "echo starting; sleep 3; exit 1"`. Watch it for two minutes with `-w`. How do STATUS and RESTARTS change?
Read the crashed run's output with `logs --previous`, and print the Pod's phase with a jsonpath query.
Repeat with `--restart=Never` and the name `once`. What are its STATUS and phase now, and why?
Delete all three Pods. Keep `pod.yaml` out of git (it was practice); the cluster stays for tomorrow.
hints: `kubectl get pod crashy -o jsonpath='{.status.phase}'` prints only the phase.

If `kind load` fails with `content digest ... not found`, Docker is using its containerd image store. Save the image with `docker image save --platform linux/arm64 -o hello.tar hello-devops:1.0.0`, then run `kind load image-archive hello.tar --name devops`.
Pod stuck in `ErrImagePull`? Check the tag, `imagePullPolicy`, and that you loaded the image into the `devops` cluster, not another one.
task.done_when: With port-forward running, `curl localhost:8000` returns JSON with `host` `hello` and `version` `1.0.0`, and you can name the phase of `crashy` (Running) and of `once` (Failed).

explain_back.prompt: Explain in 3 to 4 sentences what a Pod is and why you rarely create one by hand. Mention the shared IP address, init containers or sidecars, and what happens when a node dies.
explain_back.answer: A Pod is the smallest thing Kubernetes runs: one or more containers on one node that share an IP address and can share volumes. Most Pods have one container, and helpers come as init containers that finish before the app starts or sidecars that run beside it. Pods are disposable: if a node dies, its bare Pods are gone, and nothing recreates them. That is why you normally let a controller such as a Deployment create and replace Pods for you.

recap: A manifest has apiVersion, kind, metadata and spec; Kubernetes adds status.
Generate YAML with `--dry-run=client -o yaml` and look up fields with `kubectl explain`.
A Pod is one or more containers with one IP address; bare Pods are not replaced when they die.
Phase is one of five values; `CrashLoopBackOff` is a container state shown in STATUS, not a phase.
Init containers run first and must succeed; sidecars are init containers with `restartPolicy: Always`.
Labels are for selecting, annotations are notes, and the current context decides which cluster kubectl changes.

check.q: A Pod has two init containers and one app container. The second init container exits with code 1. What do you expect?
options: The app container starts anyway, and the error shows in its logs
The first init container runs again, then the app starts
The init container is retried, and the app never starts until it succeeds
Kubernetes deletes the Pod and schedules a new one
check.why: App containers start only after every init container exits with 0; with the default restart policy the kubelet keeps retrying the failed init container.

check.q: You want a log shipper that starts before your app and is still running when the app writes its last lines on shutdown. How do you declare it?
options: As a second entry under `containers`
As an init container with `restartPolicy: Always`
As a separate Pod with the same labels
As an init container with `restartPolicy: OnFailure`
check.why: A native sidecar is an init container with `restartPolicy: Always`, which Kubernetes starts before and stops after the app containers.

check.q: `kubectl get pods` shows nothing, but a teammate swears their Pod is running. They use namespace `payments`. What do you run first?
options: `kubectl describe nodes`
`kubectl logs payments`
`kind load docker-image payments`
`kubectl get pods -n payments`
check.why: Without `-n`, kubectl only looks in the current context's default namespace, so you must ask for the right namespace (or use `-A`).

interview.q: What is a Pod, and why does Kubernetes not just run containers?
interview.a: A Pod is a group of one or more containers that are scheduled together on one node and share a network namespace and volumes. It gives tightly coupled helpers, such as a log shipper or a proxy, a way to run next to the app with the same IP address and shared files. It also gives Kubernetes one unit to schedule, track and replace. In practice most Pods have one container and are managed by a controller such as a Deployment.

interview.q: What is the difference between an init container and a sidecar container?
interview.a: An init container runs to completion before the app containers start, in order, and must exit with code 0; it is for setup work. A sidecar runs for the Pod's whole life beside the app. Native sidecars have been stable since Kubernetes 1.33. You declare them as init containers with `restartPolicy: Always`. They start before the app, are restarted if they crash, and stop after the app. That ordering avoids losing logs or proxy traffic at start-up and shutdown.

interview.q: What is the difference between kubectl create and kubectl apply?
interview.a: The `kubectl create` command is imperative: it creates the object and fails if it already exists. The `kubectl apply` command is declarative. It creates the object if needed, or updates it to match the file. It also records what you applied in an annotation, so it can work out the changes next time. You can run apply repeatedly with the same result, which is why files in git are applied, not created. For large teams and GitOps tools, server-side apply does the same tracking on the API server.

deeper.body:
How do two containers in a Pod share one IP address? Linux namespaces, the same feature that isolates Docker containers.

When the kubelet starts a Pod, containerd first creates a tiny sandbox container, often called the pause container. Its only job is to hold the Pod's network namespace: one network interface, one IP address, one set of ports. Every container in the Pod then joins that namespace. So they share `localhost`, and two of them cannot both listen on port 80. Each container still has its own file system and its own processes. Files are shared only through volumes.

You can see the sandboxes on a kind node:
- `docker exec devops-worker crictl pods` lists Pod sandboxes.
- `docker exec devops-worker crictl ps` lists the containers inside them.

Restarts happen inside this sandbox. When a container crashes, the kubelet starts a new container in the same Pod, with the same IP address and the same volumes. An `emptyDir` volume survives a container restart, but not the Pod. That is why `kubectl logs --previous` can still find the last run: the old container's log file stays on the node until the next restart.

The STATUS column is built from several fields, in roughly this order of priority:
1. Is the Pod being deleted? Then `Terminating`.
2. Is an init container failing or still running? Then `Init:Error`, `Init:CrashLoopBackOff` or `Init:1/2`.
3. Is an app container waiting? Then its reason, such as `ImagePullBackOff` or `CrashLoopBackOff`.
4. Otherwise the phase, such as `Running` or `Completed`.

So STATUS is a summary for humans. Scripts and alerts should read the real fields: `status.phase`, `status.conditions` and `status.containerStatuses`. The `Ready` condition is what Services use to decide whether a Pod gets traffic (Day 33).

One more current detail. Kubernetes 1.35 moved finer restart rules to beta. A single container can have its own `restartPolicy`, plus rules such as "restart only if the exit code is 42". You will not need it for hello-devops. It helps batch jobs where some exit codes mean "try again" and others mean "give up".

To go further, read the [Pod lifecycle](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/) page. It is long, but it defines every word you see in the STATUS column.

title: Deployments and rollouts
goal: By the end you can run hello-devops as a Deployment, explain how its ReplicaSets heal and scale it, roll a new version out step by step, and roll back when a version is bad.

guess.q: A Deployment runs 4 Pods of version 1 with the default settings. You switch the image to version 2, but version 2 can never start. What do users notice?
options: Downtime: all old Pods stop before any new one starts
Errors: Kubernetes sends traffic to the broken Pods
Nothing: Kubernetes rolls back to version 1 on its own
Little: most old Pods keep serving, and the rollout stalls
guess.why: A rolling update removes old Pods only as far as maxUnavailable allows, and broken Pods never become ready, so they get no traffic. Kubernetes does not roll back by itself; the rollout waits until you fix it or run `kubectl rollout undo`.

terms.plain: An object that keeps a set number of identical Pods running and replaces them step by step when you change them.
The object a Deployment creates for each version of its Pod template, to keep exactly N of those Pods running.
The number of identical Pods you want, set in `spec.replicas`.
The process of moving a Deployment's Pods from one version of the Pod template to the next.
A rollout that replaces old Pods with new ones a few at a time, so the app stays up.
How many Pods above the desired count a rolling update may create at once.
How many Pods below the desired count may be unavailable during a rolling update.
A numbered version of a Deployment's Pod template that you can roll back to.

sections.h: From a bare Pod to a Deployment
sections.body:
Yesterday's Pod had no guardian. Delete it and it was gone, and a dead node would take it along. Real apps run under a **Deployment** instead. You give it a Pod template (image, ports, settings) and a number of copies. The Deployment does not create Pods itself. It works through a chain:
- Deployment: owns the update strategy and the list of past versions.
- ReplicaSet: keeps exactly N Pods from one template running.
- Pod: runs your container.

Each object points to its owner in `metadata.ownerReferences`. Delete the Deployment and the garbage collector removes its ReplicaSets and Pods too. You can follow the chain yourself: `kubectl get pod NAME -o jsonpath='{.metadata.ownerReferences[0].name}'` prints the ReplicaSet that owns a Pod.

The names tell the story. A Pod called `hello-devops-698679bfb-7l7h8` belongs to the ReplicaSet `hello-devops-698679bfb`, which belongs to the Deployment `hello-devops`. The middle part is a hash of the Pod template. Kubernetes also stores it as a label, `pod-template-hash`, on the ReplicaSet and its Pods. That label keeps the Pods of two versions apart, so their ReplicaSets never fight over each other's Pods.

You will rarely touch ReplicaSets yourself. Think of them as the Deployment's shift supervisors: one per version of the template.

sections.h: Self-healing and scaling are one loop
sections.body:
A ReplicaSet runs the control loop from Day 30 with one number in it. It counts the Pods that match its selector and compares the count with `replicas`. Too few, and it creates Pods. Too many, and it deletes some. Everything else follows from that:
- Delete a Pod by hand, and a new one appears within seconds, with a new name and a new IP address.
- Change `replicas` from 3 to 5, and two Pods appear. That is all scaling is.
- A container crashes, and the kubelet restarts it in place. The Pod still exists, so the ReplicaSet does nothing.

A dead node takes longer than most people expect. The node stops reporting, and Kubernetes marks it not ready. By default, its Pods stay bound to it for five more minutes, in case the node comes back. Only then are they evicted, and the ReplicaSet creates replacements on healthy nodes. So spread replicas over several nodes, and do not expect instant failover.

The count uses labels, not names. Remove the `app` label from one running Pod, and the ReplicaSet no longer counts it. It creates a replacement, while the relabelled Pod keeps running with no owner. Handy for pulling a Pod aside to debug it, and confusing if done by accident. For the same reason, a Deployment's `selector` cannot be changed after creation.

sections.h: What starts a rollout
sections.body:
A rollout happens if, and only if, you change the Pod template: anything under `spec.template`. These all start one:
- A new image tag, the everyday case.
- A changed environment variable, port, probe or resource setting.
- A new label or annotation inside the template.

These do not:
- Changing `replicas`. Scaling is not a new version.
- Changing labels or annotations on the Deployment itself, outside the template.
- Changing a ConfigMap that the Pods read. The template did not change, so nothing rolls (Day 34 shows the fix).

For each new template, the Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet and moves Pods from the old one to the new one. The old ReplicaSet is not deleted. It stays, scaled to 0, as a record of that version. That record is what makes rollback fast. By default the Deployment keeps the last 10 old ReplicaSets, set by `revisionHistoryLimit`.

To know before you apply whether a change will roll, run `kubectl diff -k k8s`. If the diff touches lines under `template:`, expect new Pods.

Each ReplicaSet gets a revision number in an annotation. `kubectl rollout history` lists them. Only template changes create revisions, so the history stays a clean list of versions you actually shipped.

sections.h: Rolling updates, step by step
sections.body:
The default strategy is `RollingUpdate`. Two settings control its pace:
- `maxSurge`: how many extra Pods may exist above `replicas` during the update.
- `maxUnavailable`: how many Pods may be missing below `replicas`.

Both default to 25%. Percentages are turned into whole Pods: surge rounds up, unavailable rounds down. With 4 replicas, that is 1 extra and 1 missing. So during the update you have at least 3 available Pods and at most 5 Pods in total. Both cannot be 0, or nothing could ever move.

The lab picks `maxSurge: 1` and `maxUnavailable: 0` for its 3 replicas. In words: add one new Pod, wait until it is ready, then remove one old Pod. Here is the whole update:
1. The new ReplicaSet scales to 1. There are 4 Pods: 3 old, 1 new.
2. The new Pod becomes ready. The old ReplicaSet scales to 2.
3. The new ReplicaSet scales to 2, and waits for that Pod to be ready.
4. The old ReplicaSet scales to 1, the new one to 3, and finally the old one to 0.

You never have fewer than 3 ready Pods. The price is speed and room: one extra Pod at a time needs spare CPU and memory on some node. With a big Deployment, a larger surge such as 25% finishes faster.

During the update, both versions serve traffic at once. A Service (Day 33) sends requests to every ready Pod with the right label, old or new. So version 2 must work alongside version 1, for example with the same database schema.

sections.h: Readiness decides when each step happens
sections.body:
"Wait until the new Pod is ready" carries the whole safety of a rolling update. A Pod is ready when all its containers are running and pass their readiness checks. Day 35 adds a readiness probe to hello-devops, a URL that the kubelet calls every few seconds.

Without a readiness probe, a Pod counts as ready as soon as its container starts. The app may still be loading, or broken in a way that only shows on the first request. The Deployment cannot tell, and it moves on. This is the main reason to add readiness probes before you rely on rolling updates.

When new Pods never become ready, because of a bad image or a crash at start, the rollout stalls:
- The old Pods keep serving. With `maxUnavailable: 0`, none of them is removed.
- After `progressDeadlineSeconds` (600 seconds by default), the Deployment reports the condition `ProgressDeadlineExceeded`.
- `kubectl rollout status` then exits with an error, so a CI job can notice and act.
- Kubernetes does not roll back on its own. You fix the image or run `kubectl rollout undo`.

For hello-devops, a version that crashes on start never becomes ready, and you get the stuck rollout from the worked example. A version that starts but answers every request with an error is worse. Without a probe it looks ready, and the rollout completes.

`minReadySeconds` adds one more guard. A new Pod must stay ready for that many seconds before it counts as available. That catches apps that start fine and crash a few seconds later.

sections.h: History, undo, and set image versus editing YAML
sections.body:
Four `kubectl rollout` subcommands cover most days:
- `rollout status`: follow the rollout until it finishes or fails.
- `rollout history`: list the revisions. Add `--revision=2` to see one template in full.
- `rollout undo`: go back to the previous revision, or to any kept revision with `--to-revision=N`.
- `rollout pause` and `rollout resume`: batch several changes into one rollout.

The CHANGE-CAUSE column in the history is empty unless you set the annotation `kubernetes.io/change-cause` on the Deployment, for example with `kubectl annotate`. Teams that use it write the ticket or the reason.

An undo is itself a rollout. Kubernetes copies the old template back, and the old revision moves to a new number. Revision 2 disappears from the list and comes back as revision 4.

There are two ways to change the image, and they look the same for a minute:
- `kubectl set image deployment/hello-devops web=hello-devops:1.1.0` changes the live object. Quick, and good for experiments.
- Edit `image:` in `k8s/deployment.yaml` and apply the file. Slower, but git now records the change, and someone can review it.

Mixing them causes drift. The next `kubectl apply` of an old file quietly undoes your `set image`. From Day 39, Argo CD undoes it within minutes. Experiment with `set image`, then make the real change in the file.

sections.h: Recreate: when two versions must never overlap
sections.body:
The other strategy is `Recreate`. It stops every old Pod first, and only then starts the new ones. There is always a gap with no Pods at all, so users see downtime.

That sounds bad, and for most web apps it is. Recreate exists for apps where two versions running side by side would be worse than a short outage:
- The app holds an exclusive lock, such as a single writer to a file or a queue.
- Its Pods use a disk that only one Pod can mount at a time (a ReadWriteOnce volume, Day 36).
- The new version changes the database in a way the old version cannot handle.

For hello-devops, a rolling update is right. The app is stateless, and Redis holds the shared counter, so any number of versions can run side by side.

Rolling update and Recreate are the only two strategies a Deployment has. Canary and blue-green releases need extra tools. A canary shifts traffic to the new version a little at a time, and blue-green flips all traffic at once. Argo Rollouts can do both, and so can traffic rules at a Gateway (Day 36).

analogy: Think of replacing the staff of a call center during working hours. The supervisor (the Deployment) hires one new operator, waits until they are trained and taking calls, then sends one old operator home, and repeats until the whole team is new. If the new hires keep failing training, the old team keeps working. The picture breaks on memory. A new operator can look up past calls, but a new Pod starts empty. Anything worth keeping must live outside it, the way hello-devops keeps its counter in Redis.

code.title: k8s/namespace.yaml
code.src:
# A namespace is a named folder for objects. Everything for hello-devops lives in "hello" (Day 32).

code.title: k8s/deployment.yaml (first version; Day 34 adds config, Day 35 adds probes and resources)
code.src:
# Runs 3 copies (pods) of hello-devops and replaces any that die.
# Day 32 writes this first version, Day 34 adds envFrom, Day 35 adds probes and resources.
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: hello-devops
  namespace: hello
  labels:
    app: hello-devops
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: hello-devops # must match the pod labels below
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 0 # never drop below 3 ready pods during an update
      maxSurge: 1 # add at most 1 extra pod at a time
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: hello-devops
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: hello-devops:1.0.0
          imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent # use the image kind loaded; do not pull it
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 8000

explain_back.prompt: Explain in 3 to 4 sentences how a Deployment rolls out a new image without downtime. Mention ReplicaSets, maxSurge or maxUnavailable, and readiness.
explain_back.answer: When the Pod template changes, the Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet for the new template. It scales the new ReplicaSet up and the old one down a few Pods at a time, staying within maxSurge extra Pods and maxUnavailable missing Pods. It only removes old Pods once new ones are ready, so if the new version never becomes ready, the rollout stalls while the old Pods keep serving. The old ReplicaSet stays at zero replicas, which makes `kubectl rollout undo` quick.

recap: A Deployment owns ReplicaSets, and each ReplicaSet keeps N Pods of one template running.
Self-healing and scaling are the same loop: count matching Pods, then fix the difference.
Only changes to `spec.template` start a rollout and create a revision.
maxSurge and maxUnavailable set the pace; readiness decides when each step may happen.
Stuck rollouts do not roll back on their own: use `rollout status` with a timeout and `rollout undo`.
Use `set image` to experiment, but make real changes in the YAML in git.

check.q: A Deployment has `replicas: 4`, `maxSurge: 1` and `maxUnavailable: 0`. During a rollout, what is the largest number of Pods that can exist at once?
check.why: maxSurge 1 allows one Pod above the desired 4, and maxUnavailable 0 means no old Pod leaves until a new one is ready.

check.q: You run `kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=10`. What does `kubectl rollout history deployment/web` show afterwards?
options: The same revisions as before
A new revision with the CHANGE-CAUSE `scale`
Ten new revisions, one per Pod
Only revision 1, because history resets on scale
check.why: Scaling changes `replicas`, not the Pod template, so no new ReplicaSet or revision is created.

check.q: A new version starts, passes no readiness probe (there is none), and then fails every real request. What happens during the rolling update?
options: The rollout stalls after the first Pod, so users are safe
Kubernetes notices the errors and rolls back by itself
The rollout finishes and every Pod runs the broken version
The Service skips the new Pods because they return errors
check.why: Without a readiness probe a Pod counts as ready once its container starts, so the Deployment keeps replacing old Pods with broken ones.

interview.q: How does a rolling update work in Kubernetes, and how do you roll back?
interview.a: Changing the Pod template makes the Deployment create a new ReplicaSet. It scales the new one up and the old one down within maxSurge and maxUnavailable, waiting for new Pods to be ready (and available for minReadySeconds) before going on. Old ReplicaSets are kept at zero replicas, up to revisionHistoryLimit, so `kubectl rollout undo` can scale the previous one back up. In a GitOps setup you would revert the commit instead, so git and the cluster agree.

interview.q: What is the relationship between a Deployment, a ReplicaSet and a Pod?
interview.a: A Deployment manages ReplicaSets, one per version of its Pod template, and handles rollouts and history. A ReplicaSet keeps a set number of identical Pods running by counting the Pods its selector matches and creating or deleting Pods to fix the count. Pods carry an ownerReference to their ReplicaSet and a pod-template-hash label that keeps versions apart. You normally work only with the Deployment.

interview.q: When would you use the Recreate strategy instead of RollingUpdate?
interview.a: When two versions must never run at the same time. Examples are an app that needs exclusive access to a ReadWriteOnce volume, a single-writer process, or a release that changes data in a way the old version cannot handle. Recreate stops all old Pods before starting new ones, so you accept a short outage. For stateless web services, RollingUpdate with readiness probes is almost always the better choice.

deeper.body:
How does the Deployment controller decide each step? On every pass of its loop, it works out two numbers.

The first is how many Pods may exist in total: `replicas + maxSurge`. With 10 replicas and the default 25% surge, that is 10 + 3 (2.5 rounded up) = 13. The new ReplicaSet may grow until the total of old and new Pods reaches 13.

The second is how many Pods must stay available: `replicas - maxUnavailable`. With the default 25%, that is 10 - 2 (2.5 rounded down) = 8. The old ReplicaSets may shrink only while at least 8 Pods are available.

Available is stricter than running. A Pod is available when it is ready and has stayed ready for `minReadySeconds`. So readiness, more than anything else, decides how fast a rollout moves. A rollout of a slow-starting Java service with a startup time of 40 seconds takes much longer than one of a Python service. Teams with big Deployments raise `maxSurge` to finish faster, if the nodes have room.

What if you change the template again in the middle of a rollout? The Deployment does not wait for the first rollout to finish. It creates a third ReplicaSet at once and starts scaling down both older ones. The docs call this rollover. It means a hotfix can replace a bad release that is still rolling out.

A few more fields are worth knowing by name:
- `spec.paused`: set by `kubectl rollout pause`. While paused, template changes pile up without starting a rollout. Resume, and they ship as one revision.
- `status.conditions`: `Available` and `Progressing` tell you, and your tools, how things stand. Argo CD's health check (Day 39) reads them.
- `metadata.annotations["deployment.kubernetes.io/revision"]`: the revision number on each ReplicaSet.

`kubectl rollout restart` is also a template change. It writes the current time into the annotation `kubectl.kubernetes.io/restartedAt` inside the Pod template. The template is now different, so a normal rolling update replaces every Pod. Day 34 uses this to make Pods pick up new config.

Finally, where do canary and blue-green releases fit? A Deployment cannot send 10% of traffic to a new version on purpose. During a rolling update the share of traffic follows the share of ready Pods. For controlled traffic shifting, teams use Argo Rollouts or Flagger, or weights on Gateway API routes (Day 36).

A Service type that also opens the same port, from 30000 to 32767, on every node.
An object that lists the IP addresses and ports of the Pods behind a Service, and which are ready.
The program on each node that turns Services into packet rules in the Linux kernel.

sections.h: Every Pod gets its own IP address
sections.body:
On Day 14 you met Docker networks: containers on one machine, on a private network, with ports published to the host. Kubernetes runs Pods on many machines, so its network model is bigger, and simpler to use. The rules:
- Every Pod gets its own IP address. The containers in a Pod share it.
- Every Pod can reach every other Pod by that address, on any node, with no address translation (NAT) in between.
- Programs on a node, such as the kubelet, can reach every Pod on that node.

Kubernetes itself does not build this network. A network plugin does, through a standard called CNI (Container Network Interface). The plugin hands out Pod IPs and sets up routes between nodes. kind uses a small plugin called kindnet. Clouds have plugins that give Pods real addresses in your VPC, and Calico and Cilium are popular choices elsewhere.

On kind, each node gets its own slice of the Pod range 10.244.0.0/16. `kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.podCIDR}'` prints them, for example `10.244.0.0/24 10.244.1.0/24 10.244.2.0/24`. Pods on `devops-worker` might get 10.244.1.x, and Pods on `devops-worker2` 10.244.2.x. Look at `kubectl get pods -o wide`, and you can often tell the node from the IP.

There is a catch. Pod IPs do not last. Every new Pod gets a new IP, and rollouts, scaling and failures replace Pods all the time. So never put a Pod IP in a config file. That is the problem Services solve.

sections.h: Services: one stable address for many Pods
sections.body:
A **Service** gives a changing set of Pods one stable virtual IP address and one DNS name. It finds its Pods with a label selector, just like a Deployment. The lab's `service.yaml` says, in plain words: take every ready Pod labeled `app: hello-devops`, and give them the name `hello-devops` and port 80.

Three pieces work together behind every Service:
1. The Service holds the selector and the ports. The API server gives it a virtual IP from the Service range, 10.96.0.0/16 on kind. That address is its ClusterIP.
2. A controller keeps EndpointSlices up to date. An EndpointSlice lists the IP addresses and ports of the matching Pods, and marks each one ready or not.
3. kube-proxy, on every node, reads both and writes packet rules into the node's Linux kernel.

The virtual IP lives on no network card, so `ping` gets no answer. It exists only as rules that say: traffic for 10.96.171.215 port 80 goes to one of these Pod IPs on port 8000.

Only ready Pods get traffic. A Pod that fails its readiness check keeps running, but its endpoint is marked not ready and the rules skip it (Day 35). If the selector matches no Pods, for example because of a typo in a label, the Service exists but leads nowhere. Run `kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=hello-devops` to see which case you are in. It is the first thing to check when a Service "does not work".

sections.h: Three ports: port, targetPort and nodePort
sections.body:
A NodePort Service has three port numbers, and mixing them up is the most common Service bug. Here is the lab's Service, from the outside in:
- `nodePort: 30080`: the port opened on every node. NodePorts come from the range 30000 to 32767.
- `port: 80`: the Service's own port on its ClusterIP. Other Pods call `http://hello-devops`, which means port 80.
- `targetPort: 8000`: the port on the Pod where the app listens. Leave it out and it equals `port`.

There is also `containerPort` in the Deployment. It mostly documents the port, and it lets you name it. The lab names it `http`, so a Service could say `targetPort: http` and keep working if the number ever changed.

Now follow one `curl localhost:8081` from your Mac to a Pod:
1. Docker Desktop forwards localhost:8081 into the control-plane node container, on port 30080. That is the `extraPortMappings` entry in `kind-config.yaml`.
2. kube-proxy's rules on that node catch port 30080 and pick one ready endpoint of the Service.
3. The packet goes to that Pod's IP on port 8000, possibly on another node.
4. gunicorn answers, and the reply travels back the same way.

So one mapped port on one node reaches Pods on every node. That is why kind needs only a single port mapping.

sections.h: Service types: who can reach it
sections.body:
The `type` field decides who can reach a Service:
- `ClusterIP` (the default): a virtual IP reachable only inside the cluster. Right for most services, such as Redis in the lab.
- `NodePort`: a ClusterIP, plus the same port opened on every node. Fine for labs and simple setups.
- `LoadBalancer`: a NodePort, plus a request to a cloud controller for an external load balancer with its own address.
- `ExternalName`: no proxying at all, only a DNS alias for an outside name, such as a managed database.

A headless Service sets `clusterIP: None`. It gets no virtual IP and no kube-proxy rules. Its DNS name returns the Pod IPs themselves, one record per ready Pod. Clients that must talk to each member, such as database replicas, use it. StatefulSets need one (Day 36).

LoadBalancer on a laptop needs a note. kind has no cloud, so `EXTERNAL-IP` shows `<pending>` forever. The kind project's add-on cloud-provider-kind fills that gap. On a Mac, though, the address it hands out (172.18.x.x) lives inside Docker Desktop's VM, and your Mac cannot reach it. The tool works around this with a proxy container named `kindccm-...` that publishes a port on localhost. It must run with `sudo`. For one app on your laptop, the NodePort or `kubectl port-forward` is simpler.

For HTTP traffic from users, teams rarely give every app its own load balancer. They put one Gateway in front of many ClusterIP Services (Day 36).

sections.h: How kube-proxy turns Services into packet rules
sections.body:
kube-proxy runs on every node as a DaemonSet, an object that runs one Pod per node. It does not carry traffic itself. It watches Services and EndpointSlices and programs the Linux kernel, which then sends each new connection to one Pod. It has a few modes:
- `iptables`: the long-time default, and still kind's default.
- `nftables`: the newer kernel firewall, stable since Kubernetes 1.33 and the recommended mode on new Linux nodes.
- `ipvs`: deprecated since 1.35. The plan is to switch it off by default around 1.40 and remove it around 1.43, so do not build new clusters on it.

Some network plugins, such as Cilium, replace kube-proxy and do the same job with eBPF programs in the kernel.

A few consequences matter in practice:
- Balancing happens per connection, not per request. A client that keeps a connection open (HTTP keep-alive, gRPC) can talk to one Pod for a long time. A `curl` loop opens a new connection each time, so it spreads.
- If one client must keep talking to the same Pod, set `sessionAffinity: ClientIP` on the Service. kube-proxy then pins each client IP to one Pod for a while.
- `kubectl port-forward svc/hello-devops` skips all of it. kubectl picks one Pod and tunnels to it through the API server. Good for debugging, useless for testing balance.

On kind you can see the mode in the kube-proxy ConfigMap with `kubectl -n kube-system get configmap kube-proxy -o yaml | grep mode`.

sections.h: CoreDNS and Service names
sections.body:
Inside the cluster, Pods find Services by name. CoreDNS runs as a Deployment in `kube-system`, behind a Service that is still called `kube-dns` for historical reasons. Its ClusterIP is 10.96.0.10 on kind. The kubelet writes that address into every Pod's `/etc/resolv.conf`.

Every Service gets a DNS name of this form: `<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local`. The lab's Service is `hello-devops.hello.svc.cluster.local`. You rarely type all of it, because each Pod's resolv.conf has a search list. For a Pod in namespace `hello` the list is `hello.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local`. So:
- From the same namespace, the short name works: `http://hello-devops`. That is how the app finds Redis tomorrow, with `REDIS_HOST=redis`.
- From another namespace, add the namespace: `http://hello-devops.hello`.
- The full name works from anywhere in the cluster.

A normal Service name resolves to its one ClusterIP. A headless Service name resolves to every ready Pod IP behind it, which the worked example shows. With a StatefulSet, each Pod also gets its own stable name, such as `db-0.db.hello.svc.cluster.local` (Day 36).

`cluster.local` is only a default, and a cluster admin can change it. So in app config, prefer the short name or `name.namespace`.

sections.h: NetworkPolicies: firewall rules for Pods
sections.body:
By default every Pod accepts traffic from anywhere in the cluster, and namespaces do not change that. A NetworkPolicy is a set of firewall rules for the Pods it selects. Here is how the rules work. The second one is the one people miss:
- A Pod that no policy selects allows all traffic.
- Once any policy selects a Pod for `Ingress` (incoming traffic), that Pod accepts only what some policy allows. `Egress` (outgoing traffic) works the same way.
- Policies only add permissions. There is no deny rule. You get "deny" by selecting Pods and allowing nothing.
- Rules match sources by Pod labels, namespace labels or IP ranges, plus ports. Every namespace carries the label `kubernetes.io/metadata.name` with its own name, so a rule can allow, say, the whole `monitoring` namespace.

The usual pattern has two steps. First, one deny-all policy: `podSelector: {}` selects every Pod in the namespace, with `policyTypes: [Ingress]` and no rules. Then small allow policies, one per real need. The lab's examples let anyone reach the app on port 8000 and let only the app reach Redis on 6379.

The port in a policy is the Pod's port (8000), not the Service's (80). Policies check traffic after the Service has picked a Pod.

Policies need a network plugin that enforces them. Some plugins accept the objects and silently ignore them. The kindnet plugin that kind installs does enforce them, so you can test the real thing on your laptop. Traffic from a Pod's own node is always allowed, which keeps probes working. If you ever restrict egress, allow DNS (port 53) to CoreDNS, or every name lookup fails.

analogy: A Service is like a company's main phone number. Callers dial one number and get whichever agent is free. Agents can join, leave or change desks, and nobody updates a phone book. CoreDNS is the phone book that maps the company name to that one number. A NetworkPolicy is the receptionist's list of who may be put through. The picture breaks on fairness. A phone system can route each call to the least busy agent, while kube-proxy picks a Pod per connection and does not know how busy each Pod is.

code.title: k8s/service.yaml
code.src:
# One stable name and address in front of all hello-devops pods (Day 33).
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: hello-devops
  namespace: hello
  labels:
    app: hello-devops
spec:
  type: NodePort
  selector:
    app: hello-devops # send traffic to every ready pod with this label
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80 # other pods call http://hello-devops (port 80)
      targetPort: 8000 # the port the app listens on inside its container
      nodePort: 30080 # open on every node; kind-config.yaml maps it to localhost:8081

code.title: k8s/examples/headless-service.yaml
code.src:
# Day 33: a headless Service for the same Pods as k8s/service.yaml.
# It has no virtual IP. Its DNS name returns the IP of every ready Pod instead.
#   kubectl apply -f k8s/examples/headless-service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: hello-devops-headless
  namespace: hello
spec:
  clusterIP: None # headless: no ClusterIP and no kube-proxy load balancing
  selector:
    app: hello-devops
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 8000
      targetPort: 8000

code.title: k8s/examples/netpol-deny-all.yaml
code.src:
# Day 33: block all incoming traffic to every Pod in namespace hello.
# Once a policy selects a Pod for Ingress, only traffic that some policy allows gets in.
#   Apply: kubectl apply -f k8s/examples/netpol-deny-all.yaml
#   Undo:  kubectl delete -f k8s/examples/netpol-deny-all.yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-ingress
  namespace: hello
spec:
  podSelector: {} # an empty selector picks every Pod in the namespace, new ones too
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress # and there are no ingress rules, so nothing is allowed in

code.title: k8s/examples/netpol-allow.yaml
code.src:
# Day 33: the allow rules that go with netpol-deny-all.yaml.
#   allow-web:            anyone may reach the app on port 8000 (your Mac through the NodePort, too).
#   allow-redis-from-app: only the app's Pods may reach Redis on port 6379 (Redis arrives on Day 34).
# Ports here are Pod ports (8000), not Service ports (80): policies see traffic after the Service picks a Pod.
#   Apply: kubectl apply -f k8s/examples/netpol-allow.yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-web
  namespace: hello
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: hello-devops
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
  ingress:
    - ports: # no "from" list, so any source may connect on this port
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 8000
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-redis-from-app
  namespace: hello
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: redis
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: hello-devops # only Pods with this label, in this same namespace
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 6379

Everybody, because the policies were written before the Pod existed
Only Pods labeled `app: api`, because of the allow rule

interview.q: What Service types does Kubernetes have, and when do you use each?
interview.a: ClusterIP is the default and is reachable only inside the cluster; most internal services use it. NodePort opens the same port on every node, which suits labs and simple setups. LoadBalancer asks a cloud controller for an external load balancer, the usual way to expose one TCP service in a cloud. ExternalName is only a DNS alias, and a headless Service (`clusterIP: None`) returns Pod IPs directly, which StatefulSets need. For HTTP traffic to many apps, teams put a Gateway in front of ClusterIP Services.

interview.q: How does a Service actually route traffic to Pods?
interview.a: The EndpointSlice controller watches the Pods matching the Service's selector and records their IPs, ports and readiness in EndpointSlices. On every node, kube-proxy watches Services and EndpointSlices. It programs kernel rules (iptables or nftables) that rewrite traffic for the ClusterIP or NodePort to one ready Pod. The choice is made per connection, so long-lived connections stick to one Pod. Some CNIs, such as Cilium, replace kube-proxy with eBPF.

interview.q: How do NetworkPolicies work, and what is a common pitfall?
interview.a: A NetworkPolicy selects Pods and lists allowed ingress or egress traffic by Pod labels, namespace labels, IP blocks and ports. Pods not selected by any policy allow everything; once selected for a direction, only allowed traffic passes, and policies only add permissions. A common pitfall is a default-deny egress policy that forgets DNS, so every lookup fails. Another is a CNI that does not enforce policies at all, so the YAML is accepted but has no effect.

deeper.body:
Look again at the resolv.conf from the worked example. The last line says `options ndots:5`. It changes how every name lookup in the Pod works.

ndots means: if a name has fewer than 5 dots, try the search list first. So when the app looks up `api.github.com` (two dots), the resolver first asks for:
1. `api.github.com.hello.svc.cluster.local`
2. `api.github.com.svc.cluster.local`
3. `api.github.com.cluster.local`
4. Then, finally, `api.github.com` itself.

Each try is a round trip to CoreDNS, often twice (for IPv4 and IPv6 addresses). For an app that calls outside APIs all the time, this adds load and a little latency. Two common fixes:
- Write outside names with a trailing dot, `api.github.com.`, which means the name is complete.
- Lower `ndots` for that Pod with `spec.dnsConfig.options`.

Kubernetes sets 5 so that names like `orders.shop.svc` still go through the search list. Most apps never need to touch it. It is worth knowing when someone says DNS in the cluster is slow.

A second detail: where does the client's IP address go? With a NodePort and the default `externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster`, a request can arrive on one node and be sent to a Pod on another. To make the reply come back the same way, kube-proxy replaces the source address with the node's address. Your app then logs a node IP, not the real client IP. Setting `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` keeps the client IP. The cost is that traffic only goes to Pods on the node that received it, and nodes without such a Pod drop it. Cloud load balancers handle this with health checks.

A third: Services can be dual-stack, with both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, if the cluster supports it. The kind tool can create IPv6 and dual-stack clusters from its config file. That is a cheap way to test an app before a real IPv6 rollout.

Finally, the old `Endpoints` object still exists but has been deprecated since 1.33 in favor of EndpointSlices. A slice holds at most 100 endpoints by default, so a Service with 250 Pods has three slices. Tools that read endpoints should read slices. `kubectl get endpoints` still works and prints a deprecation warning.

To see the whole picture with diagrams, read [Virtual IPs and Service proxies](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/networking/virtual-ips/) in the Kubernetes docs.

title: ConfigMaps and Secrets
goal: By the end you can give hello-devops its settings from a ConfigMap, predict when a running Pod sees a changed value, roll the Deployment to pick changes up, and explain what does and does not protect a Secret.

guess.q: Your Deployment reads `GREETING` from a ConfigMap through `envFrom`. You change the value in the ConfigMap and apply it. What do the running Pods see?
options: The old value, until the Pods are restarted
The new value, within about a minute
The new value at once, because apply restarts the Pods
No value at all, until you delete the old ConfigMap
guess.why: Environment variables are set once, when the container starts. Only files mounted from a ConfigMap are updated in place; for env vars you restart the Pods, for example with `kubectl rollout restart`.

terms.plain: An object that stores plain settings as key-value pairs, for Pods to read as env vars or files.
An object like a ConfigMap, meant for passwords, tokens and keys; its values are base64-encoded.
A container setting that turns every key of a ConfigMap or Secret into an environment variable.
A way to write any bytes as plain letters and digits; anyone can decode it, so it hides nothing.
Encrypting data where it is stored, here Secrets inside etcd, so a copy of the disk reveals nothing.
A ConfigMap with `immutable: true`, whose data can never be changed, only deleted and recreated.
